content: Vitamin poisoning, also known as hypervitaminosis, is a condition characterized by abnormally high levels of stored vitamins in the body, which can result in toxic symptoms. The specific medical term for the condition depends on the vitamin involved. For instance, an excessive accumulation of vitamin A is referred to as hypervitaminosis A. High doses of certain vitamins, such as vitamin A, slow-release vitamin B3, and very high doses of vitamin B6 (when taken alone without other B-complex vitamins), have been associated with adverse side effects. These side effects typically resolve quickly once the dosage is reduced or the supplement is discontinued. On the other hand, some vitamins, such as vitamin C, do not generally cause toxicity even at extremely high levels. For example, vitamin C has been administered in doses exceeding 100,000 mg (over 1,000 times the recommended daily intake) for the treatment of serious illnesses without causing harmful effects. However, vitamin C can have a significant laxative effect, particularly when consumed in amounts ranging from 5 to 20 grams per day in individuals who are otherwise healthy. Excessive intake of mineral supplements can also result in side effects and toxicity. Poisoning from mineral supplements, such as those containing iron, can occur but is relatively uncommon. Cases of iron toxicity have been reported due to the overconsumption of iron-containing supplements, including certain multivitamins. The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) has established tolerable upper intake levels for most vitamins to help prevent such occurrences. Fatalities due to vitamin poisoning are exceedingly rare in the United States, with no deaths typically reported in a given year. However, prior to 1998, several deaths annually were linked to pharmaceutical iron-containing supplements, particularly brightly colored, sugar-coated, high-potency iron supplements. Most of these fatalities involved children. For comparison, in 2003, there were 59 deaths attributed to aspirin poisoning and 147 deaths associated with acetaminophen-containing products. Additionally, between 1990 and 2003, an average of 54 deaths per year in the United States were caused by lightning strikes.
